item.title: Pylontech unveils all-in-one residential inverter and battery solution
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Chinese battery maker Pylontech has unveiled a new all-in-one home battery energy storage solution that provides up to 110 kWh of storage and supports up to 200% PV oversizing.
item.content:encoded:
Pylontech recently launched its Force Nex residential energy storage solution in the Australian market. The system integrates modular lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs, inverter hardware, app-based monitoring and energy control functions into a single platform.

Available in both single-phase and three-phase models, Force Nex offers single-phase configurations ranging from 4.6 to 9.9 kW, with 8–50 kWh of battery capacity. Three-phase models range from 5 to 15 kW, with 10–110 kWh of battery capacity. Customers can choose 8 kWh or 10 kWh battery modules.

Pylontech said each pack has an independent DC/DC converter, allowing compatible modules of different capacities, including new and existing Force Nex batteries, to work together.

“Homeowners can add storage as their needs grow, while keeping the batteries they already have,” the company said.

The Force Nex platform is built on LFP cells that Pylontech said have a specified cycle life of more than 10,000 cycles and 100% depth of discharge.

For rooftop solar, the range supports up to 200% PV oversizing, up to four MPPTs and 20 A input per string.

Pylontech said these features give installers more flexibility when working with different roof layouts and high-current solar panels.

“Depending on the model and system configuration, PV-to-battery charging power can reach up to 150% of the inverter’s rated power, helping store more solar energy during available sunshine hours,” the company said. “SiC (silicon carbide) technology is used in the inverters and battery DC/DC converters to support efficient power conversion and reduce energy losses.”

The Force Nex system has a built-in backup output and switches to backup power in less than 10 milliseconds, according to Pylontech. Grid pass-through current is 63 A for single-phase models and 50 A for three-phase models. The company said selected models also support up to 200% off-grid overload for 10 seconds, helping meet the short bursts of power needed when larger appliances start.

The system uses fanless cooling, with a specified noise level of 30 dB or below. IP66 protection and C5-M corrosion resistance support outdoor use, while optional battery heating supports operation in colder conditions.

Pylontech said Force Nex is designed for 10-minute installation and one-click commissioning.

“Stackable modules, guided placement, quick connections, shared grounding and handling tools simplify the physical installation,” the company said, adding that installers can connect the system through the iPylontech app, carry out setup and review its status before handover.

Pylontech said the app also allows homeowners to see how much solar power is being generated, whether the battery is charging or supplying the home, and how much electricity is being drawn from the grid.

With Force Nex now unveiled in Australia, Pylontech said it plans to launch the all-in-one energy storage system in Europe and the wider global market in the first quarter of 2027.

item.title: Why world must get serious about electrification
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: To reduce climate emissions, the world needs clean electricity powering our industry, transport, homes, lighting and heating. However, much of the energy we use still comes directly from burning fossil fuels.
item.content:encoded:
Cars burn petrol, gas heats buildings and industrial processes burn coal and gas. Currently, only 23% of global final energy demand – the energy that reaches the final user, such as households or factories – comes from electricity.

This week, at the UN climate summit COP31 in Turkey, there’s a strong focus on electrification. The COP presidency, which includes Australia’s Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Environment Minister Murat Kurum, has launched a “35-by-35” electrification pledge. They want other countries to sign on. This would see 35% of global final energy use come from electrification by 2035.

This is significant, and goes beyond switching petrol cars for electric ones. Electrification changes how we use energy, replacing the direct use of fossil fuels across transport, buildings and industry with electricity, increasingly from renewables.

However, this pledge raises a number of questions. Is this target realistic? And where did the figure of 35% come from? My colleagues and I have published analysis that provides the answers.

Why 1.5°C remains crucial

The world has run out of time to limit global warming to 1.5°C without temporarily overshooting it. The latest climate scenarios suggest that even with decisive action to cut emissions, temperatures are likely to exceed 1.5°C for at least a decade.

The latest temperature scenarios show the best we can hope for is for warming to peak around 1.7°C in the 2040s, before returning to 1.5°C by 2100. This is known as “overshoot.”

The higher and longer temperatures remain above 1.5°C, the greater the risks to people and nature. Returning to 1.5°C also requires removing large amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, something we can’t do yet at the necessary scale.

This makes the rapid reduction of emissions crucial. Rather than hoping future technologies will be able to undo the damage, we need to rely on those already available.

Why electrification matters

Electric technologies are more efficient than fossil-fuelled equivalents. An electric car converts more of its energy into movement than a petrol car. Heat pumps can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electricity consumed.

As electricity generation shifts to wind, solar and other low-emissions sources, the benefits flow into every part of the economy that uses electricity. Renewable energy reduces the emissions used to create electricity, while electrification creates more demand for renewables.

The new 35-by-35 target is intended to work alongside existing global commitments made at COP28 in Dubai three years ago; to triple renewable energy capacity and double energy efficiency by 2030.

Where does 35% come from?

Our analysis of the latest global climate scenarios finds 35% is not an arbitrary political ambition. In fact, it is the median level of electrification in climate scenarios that gives us the best remaining chance to return global warming to 1.5°C by the end of the century. The median average is the middle value in the data set.

To understand whether 35% is a credible target, we examined newly published global climate scenarios developed by the international climate modelling community.

Among these, we focused on 10 pathways with the lowest levels of warming. These would peak at around 1.7°C or less, and return to 1.5°C or below by 2100.

Across all of these projections, electricity’s share of global final energy rises from about 23% in 2025 to a median of 28% in 2030, and 35% in 2035. This shows that to align with scenarios that limit warming to 1.5°C, electricity needs to supply about 35% of the energy we use by 2035. Our research sets out the evidence.

However, the world is not yet on track. Under existing global climate policies, the International Energy Agency (IEA) projects electricity will supply just under 30% of final energy by 2035.

Of course, the climate benefit is reduced if petrol, coal and gas use is replaced with electricity generated by fossil fuels. However, the good news is that new climate scenarios show how renewable energy and electrification can work together. As renewable electricity expands, it becomes more economically viable to switch transport, buildings and industry from fossil fuels to electricity.

We have what we need

Much of the necessary technology already exists. One in four new cars sold globally in 2025 was electric according to the IEA, and up to three-quarters of global energy demand could be electrified using existing technologies.

The challenge is getting these existing technologies – such as heat pumps and electric industrial equipment – deployed. We need greater investment in electricity grids and storage, policies that encourage households and businesses to switch from gas to electrical devices, and access to affordable finance, particularly in developing countries.

There are compelling economic and security reasons to make the shift. Countries reliant on imported oil and gas are exposed when international prices spike, as we saw this year in the US-Iran conflict. Domestic renewable electricity can reduce that dependence, while efficient electric technologies lower overall energy demand.

A collective commitment

Electricity must become cleaner – reducing emissions and air pollution – as demand grows. Fossil fuel use must rapidly decline.

The 35-by-35 target is one part of a larger transformation, alongside renewable energy and energy efficiency.

The COP31 talks provide an opportunity to turn this scientific benchmark into a collective commitment. The evidence is clear that the world needs to electrify faster. The question at COP31 this week is whether governments are prepared to put the policies, investment and cooperation in place to make it happen.

Author: Anita Talberg, Honorary Fellow, Melbourne Climate Futures, The University of Melbourne. Dr Talberg works for Climate Resource, a research and science organisation that received funding from the Australian Government to prepare research and analysis to inform discussions on electrification as a COP31 priority.

This article was initially published in The Conversation and is republished here under a Creative Commons Licence.

item.title: Tongwei unveils 26.03%-efficient TOPCon solar cell with high sheet resistance
item.dc:creator: Emiliano Bellini
item.description: The solar cell was fabricated using a low-cost photoresist-based etching process to create a selective emitter with a sheet resistance of up to 1,600 Ω/sq in non-contacted regions, reducing recombination losses while maintaining effective electrical contacts. The TOPCon device achieved a certified power conversion efficiency of 26.03% and an open-circuit voltage of 746.5 mV.
item.content:encoded:
Aresearch group led by Chinese polysilicon and solar module manufacturer Tongwei has developed a tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) solar cell featuring an emitter with higher sheet resistance in a bid to reduce recombination losses, improve surface passivation and increase power conversion efficiency.

“In our work, a non-destructive photoresist-based etching process was used to form a selective emitter structure for TOPCon solar cells,” corresponding author Xiajie Meng told pv magazine. “The structure features a sheet resistance as high as 1,600 Ω/sq – to the best of our knowledge, the highest reported for TOPCon to date. This successful implementation confirms that TOPCon remains highly competitive for commercial applications.”

The researchers explained that conventional TOPCon cells face a trade-off between low contact resistance and reduced carrier recombination in the boron-doped emitter. The proposed architecture addresses this limitation by combining heavily boron-doped regions beneath the metal contacts with lightly doped regions between the contacts.

The scientists used a range of characterisation techniques to investigate the structural, electrical and passivation properties of the proposed cell architecture, with the aim of identifying optimal design conditions that balance surface passivation, lateral charge transport and metal shading losses.

They used scanning electron microscopy and 3D laser microscopy to examine etching depth and surface morphology, while four-point probe measurements determined the sheet resistance of the lightly and heavily boron-doped emitter regions. They also evaluated contact resistivity using the transmission line method and characterised doping profiles and junction depths through electrochemical capacitance-voltage measurements.

The team assessed minority carrier lifetime and emitter recombination using quasi-steady-state photoconductance measurements. Electron-beam-induced current measurements provided qualitative evidence of junction continuity, while photoluminescence imaging was used to evaluate passivation quality under different illumination levels.

Current-voltage measurements were used to determine key cell parameters, including open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current density, fill factor, efficiency and series resistance. The researchers also conducted Quokka3 simulations to compare conventional uniform emitters, selective emitters and locally boron-doped finger structures using experimentally derived parameters.

The analysis showed that that high-temperature oxidation reduced surface boron concentrations while increasing junction depth, helping suppress recombination and maintain effective metal contacts.

The scientists also found that increasing the sheet resistance of non-contacted emitter regions from 800 Ω/sq to 2,000 Ω/sq significantly improved minority carrier lifetime and surface passivation, although improvements became marginal beyond 1,600 Ω/sq, while doping uniformity deteriorated, making this value preferable for cell fabrication.

The team then compared three architectures: a conventional uniform emitter, a boron-doped selective emitter and a locally boron-doped finger structure. The selective emitter combined a sheet resistance of 450 Ω/sq beneath the metal contacts with 1,600 Ω/sq in non-contacted regions.
This configuration increased average cell efficiency from 25.82% to 25.98%, representing an absolute improvement of 0.16 percentage points.
Open-circuit voltage increased from 742.6 mV to 745.5 mV, while fill factor improved from 83.54% to 83.76%.

The optimised selective emitter cell also achieved a certified efficiency of 26.03%, with an open-circuit voltage of 746.5 mV, with the results being confirmed by Germany’s Solar Energy Research Hamelin (ISFH). The locally boron-doped finger structure also improved passivation but suffered greater fill factor losses, limiting its efficiency advantage. Its fill factor reached 83.34%, compared with 83.76% for the selective emitter, partly reflecting increased series resistance and potentially additional recombination.

The Quokka3 simulations examined the effects of contact width, grid pitch, finger width and wafer resistivity on cell performance and indicated that a contacted-region width of approximately 200 µm offered the highest efficiency among the investigated configurations. Reducing metal finger widths to 7 µm to 9 µm could enable a denser grid with a pitch of around 500 µm to 550 µm, potentially improving efficiency further, the scientists said.

“For the locally boron-doped finger architecture, simulations indicate that using silicon wafers with higher bulk resistivity alongside more closely spaced front contacts could offer opportunities for further performance improvements, although experimental validation is still required,” Meng said. “More broadly, the study demonstrates the potential of photoresist-based selective etching to produce emitters with exceptionally high sheet resistance in non-contacted areas without compromising electrical contact quality.”

The new cell concept was described in “High-efficiency TOPCon solar cells featuring super-high sheet resistance emitters via low-cost photoresist etching,” which was recently published in Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells. The research team included scientists from the School of Optoelectronic Science and Engineering, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC) and Chinese industrial equipment company Jiangsu Inspiray Equipment Co., Ltd.

“The findings could help manufacturers refine emitter doping profiles and contact designs, paving the way for further efficiency gains and potential industrial adoption of the technology,” Meng concluded.

From pv magazine Global

item.title: Recurrent wins federal approval for NSW solar and battery project
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Recurrent Energy’s plans to build a 350 MW solar farm and 600 MWh battery in New South Wales have cleared another regulatory hurdle with the federal government’s environmental watchdog providing the tick of approval for the project.
item.content:encoded:
Recurrent Energy’s Sundown solar and battery project planned for southwest New South Wales’ (NSW) New England region has been approved under the Australian government’s Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation (EPBC) Act, moving the huge project closer to construction.

Recurrent, the utility-scale solar and energy storage development platform of solar manufacturer Canadian Solar, said the Sundown project combines a 360 MW solar installation comprising about 660,000 PV panels with a 150 MW / 600 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS).

The project is being developed across a 525-hectare site about 30 kilometres east of Inverell, within the New England Renewable Energy Zone (REZ). It would connect to the National Electricity Market (NEM) via the existing 330 kV transmission line that traverses the site.

Recurrent said once operational, the facility will be capable of generating clean energy to meet the average annual electricity needs of about 176,000 households, while enhancing grid stability by supporting peak demand periods through its integrated storage solution.

“Sundown Solar Farm will play an important role in providing stability to the NSW electricity network,” the company said, adding that the electricity generated from the project will be sold to “one or more registered energy retailing organisations, large energy users or to the NEM.”

The federal nod for the Sundown solar and battery project comes after the NSW Independent Planning Commission provided its approval in August. The project secured  grid connection approval under clause 5.3.4 of the National Electricity Rules from the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) in April.

Recurrent has not yet provided a construction timeline but it is anticipated the project will support approximately 300 jobs during the peak construction period.

The Sundown solar and battery project is part of Recurrent expanding renewables portfolio. The company said it has completed the development of about 11 GW of operating utility-scale solar projects and 5 GWh of energy storage projects across six continents. It also has approximately 21 GW of solar and 76 GWh of battery storage projects under development.

Its Australia projects include the 150 MW Carwarp Solar Farm in northwest Victoria, and the 100 MW / 200 MWh Mannum BESS in South Australia. now owned by Epic Energy. Recurrent is also developing the 100 MW / 200 MW Panorama Battery project near Bathurst in western NSW.

item.title: AVL lands $15 million for relocatable vanadium electrolyte production plant
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australian Vanadium Limited has secured $15 million in state government funding to establish a relocatable vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility that will support large-scale battery installations in Western Australia.
item.content:encoded:
Perth-headquartered resources and battery technology company Australian Vanadium Limited (AVL) has executed a funding agreement with the Western Australian (WA) government for up to $15 million (USD 10.38 million) to establish a relocatable vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility.

AVL said the funding will support the design, construction and commissioning of a high-capacity vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility utilising the company’s V-Nomad production platform.

Designed as a relocatable solution, the V-Nomad platform allows for electrolyte to be manufactured at or near project sites for GWh-scale vanadium flow battery (VFB) installations. The platform is intended to cut logistics, storage and commissioning costs, and support multiple vanadium feedstocks.

AVL Chief Executive Officer Graham Arvidson said the project will expand its capacity to produce vanadium electrolyte to support large-scale VFB projects as well as increasing local content in the vanadium flow battery supply chain.

“The awarding of this grant is an important milestone for AVL and recognises the progress we have made in developing vanadium electrolyte manufacturing capability in Western Australia,” he said.

“The grant will support the next stage of development of our V-Nomad platform and our broader strategy of integrating Western Australian vanadium production, electrolyte manufacturing and utility scale vanadium flow battery deployment, including through opportunities pursued by our downstream business, VSUN Energy.”

The WA government will contribute up to 50% of the project cost, capped at $15 million, with AVL funding the balance.

WA Development Minister David Michael said the project presents an opportunity for the state to further invest in energy transition initiatives by supporting grid-scale energy storage and strengthening critical minerals supply chains.

“By supporting AVL’s electrolyte manufacturing capability, we’re creating new opportunities in advanced manufacturing while helping position WA at the forefront of long-duration energy storage technologies,” he said.

“The development of a high-capacity vanadium electrolyte facility will support local jobs, strengthen our manufacturing capability, and provide the foundations for future grid-scale battery projects across the state.”

The downstream initiative is supported upstream by AVL’s namesake project at Gabanintha in the state’s mid-west, which hosts a mineral resource estimate of 395.4 million tonnes at 0.77% vanadium pentoxide. 

The funding has been awarded through the WA government’s Investment Attraction Fund (IAF).

item.title: Home battery volumes on rise as rebate tally reaches 600,000
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australia’s small-scale battery energy storage market is on the rise with the latest data from industry analyst SunWiz revealing that more than 1 GWh of capacity was installed nationwide in October, up almost 10% compared to the previous month.
item.content:encoded:
The latest report from SunWiz shows Australian households and businesses installed an estimated 1,043 MWh of battery energy storage (5-100 kWh) capacity in October 2026, up 9.7% on the 966.5 MWh registered in September and the strongest month since April’s 3,262 MWh peak. The October tally is about 18% more than the 885 MWh registered in the same month last year.

SunWiz Managing Director Warwick Johnston said the market is making a “steady recovery” after changes made to the federal government’s Cheaper Home Batteries rebate scheme. Those changes, introduced in May 2026, included a scaling of the incentive across small, medium and large systems.

“This is the second straight rise after August’s small dip, and volumes are now nearly double the May low, though still about 68% below April,” he said.

“[This is a] continuation of recovery after [the] post-April slump, as customers come to the market in their own time, and in preparation for summer.”

Johnston said growth came mostly from systems sized at 20 kWh and above, with the 20-30 kWh segment accounting for 399 MWh of the month’s total capacity, ahead of 40-50 kWh at 273 MWh and 30-40 kWh at 210 MWh.

“Together, the bands from 20 kWh upward made up 85% of capacity,” he said. “At the smaller end, 10-20 kWh rose 3% to 150 MWh and 0-10 kWh was flat at 11 MWh.”

The national average system size rose to 26.74 kWh, its fifth consecutive monthly gain.

Johnston said average system sizes have climbed steadily since May’s low of about 22 kWh but are still well below April’s 36.6 kWh peak.

Most states and territories posted growth in battery installations in October with 356 MWh of new capacity registered in New South Wales alone, up 10% on the previous month.

Installations in Victoria climbed 17% to 227 MWh while Queensland was up 5% to 217 MWh.

The release of the SunWiz data was followed by Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen revealing that more than 600,000 batteries have now been installed under the government’s Cheaper Home Batteries program.

Bowen said more than 600,000 residential and business battery energy storage systems, representing close to 16.6 GWh of storage capacity, have been installed across Australia since the introduction of the rebate program on 1 July 2025.

“[This] makes us now second in the world for home batteries; more home batteries than China, more home batteries than India, more home batteries than the United States, more home batteries than France, more home batteries in the United Kingdom, second only to Germany,” he said, adding that more than 75% of batteries installed under the program have been in outer suburban and regional communities.

item.title: Australia’s data centre pipeline provides food for thought
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: There is no shortage of opinion about data centres right now: where they should go, how they should be powered and what they will do to the grid. The industry has the potential to drive new renewable energy demand but could also trigger grid strains if the rollout is not well managed. Here's a closer look at the numbers and some signals Australia’s development pipeline shows as of October 2026.
item.content:encoded:
RenewMap is currently tracking more than 276 active data centre projects across Australia: 150 operating (about 2 GW), 30 under construction (about 3.7 GW), and 96 in development (about 31 GW). One caveat up front: the project size in MW RenewMap tracks is a project’s connection capacity, not the IT load it will draw at any one moment, which is lower.

A step change in scale

When we look at the fleet of operating data centres today, the average size sits around 20MW a site. Data centre projects currently under construction are seven times larger on average, and those in the development phase about 19 times larger in connection size in MW.

A small 10 MW facility can fit into the existing grid without much fuss. A development-stage campus in the many hundreds of megawatts or gigawatt scale needs its own generation, which is why so much of the current energy debate centres on new large loads. The Clean Energy Investor Group’s latest Clean Energy Outlook report found 92% of investors expect data centres to be positive for clean energy investment. The federal government’s new data centre standards and regulatory reforms point the same way: new large loads will be required to bring new firmed renewable energy to supply their massive energy consumption needs.

Most of the development pipeline is pre-planning

Of the capacity in development, only about 2.4 GW across 20 projects has planning approvals in place. Around 9.8 GW across 31 projects is currently under assessment, and roughly 19 GW across 29 projects has not been submitted for approval at all. By megawatts, more than half of the proposed capacity has not yet reached a planning department. Another caveat, a number of early stage projects have not yet published a connection size, so if anything the real total is understated.

These are projects with capital committed to progressing through planning, so the pipeline is real, but the majority of it is in early stages. Plans also change, in the 2026 Electricity Statement of Opportunities (ESOO), Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) stated that 36% of the data centre projects in its 2025 pipeline were later cancelled, some with connections already in place. What we can take from this is that whilst there is a lot of activity and a huge pipeline of projects, not all of these will get built.

Data centre pipeline is heading regional

Another critical trend we’ve been following is the shift of large data centres from metro areas in Sydney and Melbourne, to regional locations. Virtually no regional data centre capacity is operating or under construction today, but the regions now hold the majority of the development pipeline.

So what’s driving the regional shift? Today’s data centres had to be near people, with low latency. What’s being proposed are data centres running large-scale AI training and inference workloads. The projects are power-hungry, but have less requirements for low latency, so developers are chasing sites in regional areas, where land and grid capacity are more available. Much of the regional pipeline is also positioning in brownfield sites, like former coal regions or industrial areas where large grid connections already exist, or in declared Renewable Energy Zones.

Measured by capacity, 98% of operating data centres and 97% of those under construction sit in metropolitan areas. In the development pipeline, that flips: 58% of proposed capacity is regional.

The regional examples are concrete, and many are already in our data. CDC’s Wagga Wagga campus in regional NSW (1,400 MW) is one of the largest single projects we track. Alongside IREN’s recently announced Redbank Data Centre (900MW), an additional 1.4GW of new battery developments and the new 500KV HumeLink transmission line, this small region on the southern outskirts of Wagga Wagga is becoming a hotbed of development.

However, recent media attention and community push back has placed increased scrutiny on large data centre projects. Developers are looking to earn social licence from host communities, in the same way wind, solar and BESS developers already do. We’ve already seen recent media announcements on the sheer scale of community benefit proposed (CDC up to $225 million and IREN greater than $200m going to the local council over 30 years for these two projects near Wagga Wagga).

We’re seeing similar large-scale projects proposed across a number of other states and territories:

  • In Victoria’s Latrobe Valley, EnergyAustralia’s Yallourn 1 and 2 (1,000 MW each) and Keppel’s Morwell (720 MW) are landing on the site of a retiring coal region.
  • In the New South Wales Hunter region, there is the Hunter Valley AI Training Campus (1,000 MW) and the Mayfield Energy Precinct at Newcastle (1,000 MW). Wallerawang near Lithgow (1,000 MW) is another former coal-power site.
  • In Queensland, Zerra DC’s Western Downs Digital Park near Chinchilla in Queensland runs up to 2,160 MW across four stages, with Anthropic already signing a long term lease for running AI inference workloads answering user queries.
  • South Australia there is IREN’s Bundey Data Centre Campus (800 MW) and the Aurora Energy Precinct (200 MW). Several are co-developed by parties you would not have associated with data centres a few years ago, including mining companies, battery developers and independent power producers, and most have not yet lodged a development application.
  • Project Ares and the Beetaloo Digital Data Centre are pushing into genuinely remote parts of the Northern Territory

Development approval timeframes vary greatly, state-by-state

One interesting aspect we’re tracking in the data is how long approval takes across different states and assessment pathways. As an example, a data centre planning application in New South Wales takes on average about nineteen months to be approved. Compared to Victoria, where it takes about five months on average. That gap is already shaping where developers are choosing to site projects. More development applications were submitted in Victoria over the past six months than in any other state, and given the timeframes involved, the pipeline is starting to tilt toward Victoria. Speed to market is critical for these projects.

If we drill into the five most recently approved projects across these two states, Victorian planning approvals took anywhere from two to six months. By comparison, in New South Wales, the five most recent approvals took between nineteen months to more than two years.

Time from lodgement to approval for Victoria’s five most recently approved data centres, in monthsTime from lodgement to approval for NSW’s five most recently approved data centres, in months.

Who are the key players getting projects built?

Capacity that is currently operating or under construction is concentrated among a few providers, led by CDC, AirTrunk and NEXTDC. For the leaders, most of that capacity is still under construction rather than live, so the jump in scale is being driven by a small number of players committing to large projects.

The development pipeline tells its own story, and the names leading it are not all traditional data centre operators. The familiar co-location players are there, with NEXTDC, CDC and Zerra DC all proposing large campuses. But they now sit alongside two newer groups. The first is the neocloud providers, AI compute specialists such as Firmus and IREN, several of them repurposed from crypto mining, chasing cheap power at scale. The second is the energy and infrastructure sector itself, with EnergyAustralia, Syncline Energy, Malabar Resources, Greenspot and others developing projects directly. It is a signal that the next wave of capacity is being shaped as much by power and land as by compute infrastructure.

What to take from it?

A few findings stay constant across every cut of the data. The data centres being proposed are far larger than the ones already built and new capacity is increasingly following energy projects into the regions. The time taken to approve a data centre varies widely by state, taking more than three times as long for projects in New South Wales to get approved, compared to Victoria. How much of the capacity will get built? Most is not yet approved, some will fall away and the regional shift depends on grid capacity, fibre networks and workforce that is not yet in place. But more broadly, the shift will depend on projects being well received by regional communities and developers gaining social licence to develop in these areas.

We will keep tracking it project by project. RenewMap covers 4,500+ utility-scale energy projects and large loads across Australia and New Zealand, from early feasibility through to operations, across more than 100 data fields updated daily by our analysts in Australia.

Author: Alex Thompson, co-founder, RenewMap

item.title: SunDrive targets space applications with copper solar cell tech
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: SunDrive Solar, the developer of unique copper-based PV technology, has joined forces with Sydney-based space hardware and software manufacturer Space Machines Company to develop Australian-made solar arrays for spacecraft.
item.content:encoded:
Australian solar cell technology innovator SunDrive Solar has teamed with Space Machines Company (SMC) to accelerate the development of its copper-based heterojunction (HJT) solar cell technology, aiming to establish a source of Australian-made solar arrays for commercial spacecraft and satellites.

Spun out of the University of New South Wales (UNSW), SunDrive has developed a proprietary copper electroplating technology that replaces silver in solar cell metallisation, aiming to reduce manufacturing costs and improve efficiency.

The company’s cells, which have delivered record-breaking results, are ultra-thin and lightweight, qualities that SunDrive co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Vince Allen said matter in orbit, where every gram of array mass is a trade against payload.

“SunDrive’s copper HJT technology brings together the ultra-thin, lightweight and high-efficiency performance needed for next-generation spacecraft solar arrays,” he said. “And applying that to SMC’s Optimus Viper program is a great opportunity to demonstrate what Australian innovation can achieve in the demanding environment of Low Earth Orbit.”

Under the research and development collaboration SunDrive will work with SMC, which is focused on developing sovereign space transportation capabilities for Australia, to produce a body-mounted solar panel for the company’s Optimus Viper spacecraft, a 200 kg vehicle designed for autonomous operations across Low Earth Orbit.

SunDrive will lead cell selection, module design, lamination and electrical characterisation. SMC will lead substrate design, structural and thermal analysis of the panel, assembly and testing, and mounting the panel on a structural model of Optimus Viper. The two companies will jointly develop the process for bonding solar modules to the panel substrate.

The parties said the body-mounted panel will be subjected to environmental testing, including thermal-vacuum and vibration testing, which will produce the engineering and performance data needed to move towards a flight-ready solar array.

SMC co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Rajat Kulshrestha said solar arrays are among the most critical and costly parts of any spacecraft and Australian satellite programs currently depend on imported space-grade arrays, which limits both cost and supply.

“This collaboration began because two Australian companies saw a commercial reason to work together,” he said. “Other nations are moving quickly to secure their space supply chains, and partnerships like this are how Australia builds capability that lasts.”

SunDrive CEO Natalie Malligan said demand is growing for power systems that are high-performance, resilient, lightweight and scalable and both companies want more of that value chain to stay in Australia.

“As the global space economy rapidly accelerates, Australia is well-placed to seize the opportunity, not just to participate, but to build and own the critical technologies that will underpin it,” she said.

item.title: Longi achieves 35.31% efficiency in perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell based on self-assembled molecules
item.dc:creator: Emiliano Bellini
item.description: Longi has developed a perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell with a certified efficiency of 35.25% by using specially engineered molecules to improve interface quality and charge extraction. The device also demonstrated enhanced operational stability, retaining 94% of its initial efficiency after 1,500 hours of continuous operation.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese solar module manufacturer Longi has developed a perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell using specially designed molecules that suppress excessive molecular stacking while maintaining efficient charge transport.

“This molecular design promotes the formation of a uniform, well-organized self-assembled monolayer (SAM), even on rough, pyramid-textured surfaces,” Longi researcher Bo He told pv magazine. “By balancing molecular packing and surface coverage, the engineered interface improves energy-level alignment for faster charge extraction, reduces defects through molecular flexibility, and provides a stable foundation for the growth of high-quality perovskite films.”

The researchers explained that conventional SAM molecules often suffer from excessive aggregation, resulting in uneven coverage on textured silicon surfaces. To address this limitation, they designed molecules with controlled molecular twisting and conjugation. They developed four SAM derivatives – TC0, TC1, TC2 and TC3 – based on the commonly used 4PACz molecule.

TC2 offered the best balance between molecular packing, substrate adhesion and charge transport, as its structure combines a conjugated backbone with a moderately twisted phenyl side group. Molecular simulations showed surface coverage of 83.1%, compared with 75.0% for TC1 and 73.3% for TC3. Experimental measurements confirmed that TC2 achieved more than 80% coverage and exhibited strong anchoring stability.

The improved molecular arrangement also enhanced the electronic properties of the interface between the indium tin oxide (ITO) layer and the perovskite absorber. In particular, TC2 modified the ITO work function and provided favorable energy-level alignment for efficient hole extraction. This strengthened the internal electric field, accelerating charge separation and transport, while improved interface coverage reduced defects and suppressed charge recombination.

The analysis also showed that TC2 promoted slower, more controlled perovskite crystallisation, producing larger, more uniform grains with higher crystallinity. The resulting films exhibited improved phase uniformity and reduced nonradiative recombination. Photoluminescence measurements showed a quantum yield of 1.46% and a quasi-Fermi level splitting of 1.292 eV, the highest values among the tested SAMs.

Using this molecular engineering approach, the researchers fabricated a two-terminal monolithic tandem solar cell combining a perovskite top cell with a heterojunction (HJT) bottom cell.

The device features a textured silicon bottom cell coated with an ITO recombination layer, followed by a TC2-based SAM serving as the hole-selective contact. The perovskite absorber is deposited on the SAM and covered with a lithium fluoride (LiF) interlayer, a fullerene (C60) electron transport layer and a tin oxide (SnOx) buffer layer. The stack is completed with a transparent indium zinc oxide (IZO) electrode, a silver (Ag) contact and a magnesium fluoride (MgFx) optical coating.

Under standard test conditions, TC2-based devices achieved an average open-circuit voltage of 2.007 V and a fill factor of 84.30%, outperforming cells based on 4PACz, TC1 and TC3. The champion device reached a power conversion efficiency of 35.31%, with a short-circuit current density of 20.82 mA/cm2, an open-circuit voltage of 2.007 V and a fill factor of 84.53%.

Independent testing by China’s National Center of Inspection on Solar Photovoltaic Products Quality (CPVT) certified a reverse-scan efficiency of 35.25%, a fill factor of 84.98% and a stabilized efficiency of 35.13%. External quantum efficiency measurements confirmed effective light absorption and current generation in both subcells.

Stability tests also demonstrated improved resistance to light-induced degradation and phase segregation in TC2-based perovskite films. The tandem devices retained 94% of their initial efficiency after 1,500 hours of continuous operation under the ISOS-L-1 protocol and 82% after 1,000 hours at 65 C under the ISOS-L-2 protocol.

“Overall, the results demonstrate that optimized molecular interface engineering can simultaneously improve the efficiency, charge transport and operational stability of perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells,” He said.

The cell technology is described in “Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells,” published in Nature. Researchers from China’s Soochow University, Northwestern Polytechnical University and Hong Kong Polytechnic University participated in the study.

The new development builds on a series of advances in molecular interface engineering for perovskite photovoltaics. In September, an international research team involving Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Northwestern Polytechnical University developed a symmetry-breaking molecular strategy that improved SAM coverage by combining symmetric and asymmetric molecules. The resulting inverted perovskite solar cell achieved an efficiency of 26.32%, with a certified value of 25.67%, while retaining 93% of its initial performance after 1,150 hours of operation.

In December 2025, researchers led by Northwestern Polytechnical University developed a perovskite-silicon tandem cell with a certified efficiency of 31.71%. Their approach relied on chemical polishing to selectively remove residual lead iodide from the perovskite absorber, reducing recombination losses and improving film uniformity. Around the same time, a team led by Soochow University achieved 32.3% efficiency using a steric-complementary interface design combining small, flexible molecules for defect passivation with larger molecules providing protection against environmental degradation. The device achieved a certified efficiency of 32.12%.

More recently, Longi and Soochow University developed a 34.0%-efficient tandem cell using a dual-anchored interface incorporating zirconium oxide (ZrO2) nanoparticles between the transparent conductive oxide and the SAM. The approach reduced interfacial recombination and leakage while maintaining efficient charge extraction. The device achieved an open-circuit voltage of 1.997 V and retained 84% of its initial efficiency after 2,000 hours of operation.

Longi has also continued to advance tandem cell efficiency. In April 2025, the manufacturer achieved a certified efficiency of 34.85% for a two-terminal perovskite-silicon device, using a bilayer passivation strategy based on lithium fluoride and ethylenediammonium diiodide. In July 2026, the company raised its tandem cell efficiency record to 35.5%, with the result independently certified by the European Solar Test Installation (ESTI).

Alongside its tandem research, Longi has made progress in conventional crystalline silicon technology. In November 2025, the company disclosed the technical details of its 27.81%-efficient silicon solar cell, based on a hybrid interdigitated back-contact architecture combining passivated tunneling contacts, dielectric passivation layers and optimized carrier transport.

From pv magazine Global

item.title: Sodium-ion batteries approach cost parity with LFP, with 70 GWh covered by supply agreements
item.dc:creator: Pilar Sánchez Molina
item.description: Sodium-ion batteries are approaching cell-level cost parity with LFP technology, with supply agreements exceeding 70 GWh worldwide. Despite higher upfront costs, they could offer a 21% lower total cost of ownership over 20 years, according to Wood Mackenzie.
item.content:encoded:
Sodium-ion battery technology is entering the commercial production phase and emerging as an alternative to lithium-ion batteries, driven by supply chain diversification, strong low-temperature performance, and the potential for lower total cost of ownership. According to an analysis by Wood Mackenzie, supply agreements totaling more than 70 GWh are already in place.

The study, which examines markets in China, the United States, Germany, and India, identifies sodium-ion batteries as the most promising emerging alternative to lithium-based technologies for stationary energy storage. Leading manufacturers are expected to achieve cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries by late 2026, while parity at the module and system levels is not expected until after 2030.

China is leading the commercialisation of the technology. BYD plans to reach 30 GWh of sodium-ion battery manufacturing capacity, while CATL aims to exceed 1 GWh in sodium-ion battery shipments by the end of 2026.

Supply agreements for sodium-ion batteries are already in place in China, the United States, and Europe, while India remains in the early stages of commercial validation. For the 2026–2035 period, Wood Mackenzie estimates a learning rate of 18% to 20% in China, reflecting the greater maturity of its industrial supply chain.

Planned manufacturing capacity currently exceeds demand, although the growing number of supply agreements points to the technology’s gradual adoption in the market.

Higher upfront costs, lower total cost of ownership

Sodium-ion batteries currently have higher upfront costs than LFP batteries. The global average stands at $333/kWh (USD 229), compared with approximately $290/kWh (USD 200) for LFP batteries. However, Wood Mackenzie estimates that sodium-ion batteries could achieve a 21% lower total cost of ownership over a 20-year project lifetime.

The difference is primarily attributed to the elimination of capacity expansion cycles and lower operating costs. The economics of sodium-ion systems remain relatively stable across storage durations of two to four hours.

The study identifies raw material supply security, service life, and a wider operating temperature range as key technical advantages of sodium-ion batteries. The latter could make them particularly suitable for applications in cold climates, where lithium-ion batteries may require additional thermal management systems.

Regulation accelerates development

Industrial and trade policies are playing an increasingly important role in the competitiveness of different battery chemistries. In July 2026, China reintroduced a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries while exempting sodium-ion batteries until the end of 2028. LFP batteries became subject to a 2% levy in September 2026, which is set to increase to 4% in September 2027.

In the United States, tariffs of approximately 58% on energy storage cells imported from China, combined with production tax credits under Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), are encouraging domestic sodium-ion battery manufacturing.

In Europe, carbon footprint declaration requirements under the EU Battery Regulation could favor technologies with supply chains that are less dependent on certain critical raw materials. Meanwhile, India is supporting domestic manufacturing through a $1.25 billion incentive program and tariff exemptions for certain types of manufacturing equipment.

Wood Mackenzie expects the 2030–2035 period to be decisive for sodium-ion batteries to achieve economic competitiveness. For energy storage projects currently under development, LFP remains the most commercially mature option for storage durations of two to four hours.

From pv magazine Global
